title: Skills are the New SDKs - Elvin Aghammadzada, DataRobot
talk_summary: Elvin Aghammadzada argues that context is a limited budget that degrades past ~25-40% usage, and that 'skills' (progressive-disclosure markdown files with front-matter metadata, a body, and optional scripts) are a cheaper, more reliable alternative to dumping tools/instructions into the system prompt. He contrasts skills with MCP (skills for reasoning/thinking, MCP for auth, isolation, and heavy remote execution) and warns that LLM-generated skills and unvetted skill marketplaces are risky.

takeaways.technique: Progressive disclosure via skill front-matter index
takeaways.what_they_do: Only a small front-matter block (<100 tokens) is loaded into the system prompt as an index; the full skill body (<5K tokens) loads only when the agent decides it needs it, and scripts run externally with only output returned to context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this is only thing that's loaded to the agent's context... the second one, on activation, which is typically less than 5K tokens
takeaways.numbers: front matter <100 tokens; body <5K tokens; 15 MCP servers ~100K tokens/session vs ~10x smaller with skills

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat context as a budget: keep pre-work context well under ~40% of the window so the agent doesn't start in the 'dumb zone'; trim irrelevant files, web searches, and error messages that drag attention.
takeaways.evidence_quote: after 25% usage of the context window... the performance starts to degrade

takeaways.technique: Skills vs MCP split by job
takeaways.what_they_do: Use skills when the hard part is reasoning/how-to-think; use MCP when you need auth, process isolation, or heavy remote compute (GPUs, huge datasets). Skills can wrap/expose an MCP server and do progressive disclosure for it.

takeaways.technique: Version, test, and evaluate skills as software
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat skills as code: version them, evaluate and test them, and prefer human-authored skills because LLM-generated skills were found to use more tokens and reason longer without improving speed or context use.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the LM generated skills hurts the performance of LM in a sense that it uses more tokens

takeaways.what_they_do: Skills run in the agent's own environment with no process isolation, and marketplaces lack verification, so third-party or LLM-written skills are a prompt-injection and trust risk (analogous to early NPM).
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is no isolation... these marketplaces still lack the verification control

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of building separate agents per domain, keep one capable general-purpose agent with ~10 tools and layer domain skills on top; use sub-agents to keep context clean.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this is just a coding agent that has access to about 10 tools, which can do anything for you, as long as you have skills on top of it
